entries.title: #I'm Looking For a Zombie
entries.jpTitle: #ゾンビさがしてます

review.en:
Episode #4: I'm Looking for a Hospital

"Without a doubt, one of the dark horses of the season? Or rather, one of the precious few genuinely watchable shows in the barely surviving Fall 2026 lineup."

This show might just turn out to be the dark horse of the season... Seriously. Back in Episode 1, I remember thinking, "What the hell is wrong with these goofy, carefree idiots? Do they have any sense of danger at all?" But now I'm realizing that those doubts were completely justified—and that the characters really were that clueless and lacking in any sense of urgency. And that's precisely what makes this show feel so believable. With each passing episode, that sense of realism grows stronger, and as a viewer, you can actually feel it happening. Every time I watch, I find myself thinking, "Yeah... this is what a post-apocalyptic world would really be like." And I think that's absolutely brilliant.

I also love how the know-it-all, levelheaded character, who had been rubbing me the wrong way for quite some time, is finally treated as someone who matters—accepted for who she is, including the very qualities she herself has always wanted to embody. Then there's the MC, whose blunt sense of right and wrong, moral convictions, and understanding of what truly matters to people hit all the harder precisely because she's only recently stepped out into the real world. And in the middle of all this, when one of their companions suffers a terrible injury that might even turn her into a zombie, they're casually throwing around lines like, "Hungry? Want something to eat? How about some human flesh?" That kind of dark, offhand humor is fantastic. I'm increasingly realizing just how much thought has gone into practically every aspect of this show's storytelling and characterization.

Of course, I still find it a little hard to believe that they could go through everything at the hospital this episode and simply be released without anything being done to them. But hey, as long as the story eventually gives me a convincing reason to accept that, I'm willing to let it slide for now. So yes, this episode gets a 10 from me, although I'm keeping its WRP score relatively conservative.
review.jp:
第4話: 病院さがしてます

"間違いなく今期のダークホース?というか瀕死の2026秋シーズンの数少ない見るに耐える作品"

『本作は今期のダークホースになる・・・かも?知れない。第1話で感じた、"何このふざけたおちゃらけ連中?危機感あるの?"といったものは、現時点では至極納得のいく疑問であり、事実でもあったことが分かった。だからこそ本作に現実味があり、それが話を増すごとに増していき、それを見てる側が感じ、見るごとに"これが終末なんだな"と思える・・・それが素晴らしいと思った。ずっと感じの悪かった何でも知ってるしっかりもののキャラが欲しかった自分そのものの存在を受け入れてちゃんとそこに"あるもの、大事なもの"として扱ってくれることや、MCの最近現実の世界に出てきたからこそ余計にぶちかましてしまう正論というか倫理観と言うか人にとって大事なものも響く。そこでゾンビになってしまうかも知れない大怪我を負った（負わせた）仲間に「お腹すいた?なんか食べたい?人食べたい?」みたいな軽口が飛び交うのも非常にいい・・・。あらゆる描写がちゃんと考えられていることにも気付かされる・・・。もちろん、今回の病院でのやり取り、何もされずに解放されるというのはちょっとありえないだろうとも思えるが、まぁそれも今後納得がいけばいいかな・・・。ということもあり10点だがWRPとしては控えめ。』

The story begins when Aki, who has no memories of the world before its fall, escapes her village with her close friends Haru and Natsuki to search for her missing father. As they venture into the outside world, they find themselves surrounded by zombies on all sides! Along the way, they rescue Yuu and Sakura and take refuge in a home improvement store. They regroup, and now the counterattack begins—!!

review.en:
Episode #4: Eleonora

"An outstanding episode that finally makes the characters' distinctive traits and unusual nicknames click, while bringing the show's uniquely delicate storytelling to life."

The way this episode portrays all those seemingly insignificant yet meaningful exchanges, gestures, and reactions scattered throughout is simply superb. There's something incredibly appealing about Eleonora's rugged, blunt, and rather unrefined personality, especially when contrasted with her subtle femininity. At the same time, the episode gradually builds an unsettling sense that their stay here might somehow have been deliberately arranged, and I love how that underlying uncertainty quietly creeps into the story.

It's also an episode that gives nicknames like "the boy who isn't sleepy" a much clearer sense of meaning, making those unusual ways of referring to the characters feel increasingly natural and significant. I really appreciate how even something as simple as a nickname becomes an effective part of the storytelling. All in all, this episode left me thoroughly impressed, with one delightful little touch after another. I genuinely can't wait to see what happens next—and this is one of the precious few shows this season that actually makes me feel that way.

『そこかしこに散りばめられる些細だが重要なやり取りや仕草や反応の数々が秀逸に描かれている。エレオノーラのなんとも無骨でぶっきらぼうな性格と女性らしさがなんとも言えずよい。また、この滞在が何かしら仕組まれたもの?と感じる危うさもじわじわと感じさせるように描かれていてそれもまた良し。眠くない君といいった呼び方がより意味をなす様な話しでもあり、そういった呼称が良い味付けとなる演出もあったりと、感心と好感触に溢れる回だった。続きが気になる。そんな気持ちになる今期数少ない作品である。』

review.en:
Episode #3: Woking is…Hard Work.

"Surprisingly well-crafted, with some genuinely thoughtful character development and a satisfying sense of progression... The odds of me staying on board all the way to the final stop just went up!"

This was really good. Once the trip to Nagasaki was decided, I figured she'd need money for the journey, so maybe she'd get a part-time job and we'd be treated to some cute, carefree antics? But instead, we get a string of hilariously pathetic failures that eventually leads her to a job connected to the railway. What impressed me was how the show actually took the time to depict the entire process—something that feels surprisingly rare these days. Her determination, the little ways she shows consideration for her mother along the way, and the portrayal of her father all feel carefully thought out.

I especially appreciated how she earns recognition through genuine effort, gradually discovers that everyone has their own strengths and weaknesses, and finds a job that actually suits her—adding yet another meaningful connection to the world of railways. That sense of building something step by step was really satisfying. And the fact that she uses her very first paycheck to buy her mother a thoughtful, practical gift rather than something extravagant? That was wonderful. Man, I'm such a sucker for this kind of thing... This show might actually turn out to be a surprisingly good one!

review.en:
Episode #3

"Not particularly original, but everything clicks beautifully in this outstandingly entertaining episode featuring Maria Naganawa, Robo-kun, and an Initial D parody!"

Man, this was hilarious. Robo-kun, voiced by Maria Naganawa, is admittedly a pretty familiar type of character, and the storyline itself isn't exactly groundbreaking either. He starts out as a model robot, gradually goes over to the dark side, gets fired and sent off to work at a family restaurant... and eventually turns over a new leaf and starts teaming up with the MC. It's all been done before in one form or another, but somehow, every step of the way is packed with this wonderfully understated humor that just works.

The Initial D parody was great, of course, but what impressed me even more were all the clever little comedic touches scattered throughout the episode. The overall pacing, the character interactions, the timing of the jokes—everything was spot-on. Could this show end up being one of the saviors of this otherwise painfully lackluster, downright disastrous anime season? Whatever the case, I'm just grateful we've got something this entertaining to watch!
review.jp:

review.en:
Episode #4: Remission / The Closure That We Needed

"Enough with these ridiculous coincidences already! Koyun is just an incredibly self-absorbed, narcissistic pain in the ass... Man, she's exhausting."

I do think the storytelling is incredibly skillful, though. It's just that I've become increasingly allergic to convenient coincidences lately... Someone happens to run into the exact person they were just thinking about, at precisely the right moment. Then there's this scene where someone heads to a nearby convenience store in the middle of the day, wearing what looks like loungewear—or pajamas?—to buy some ice cream, and just as they reach for it, the other person, also apparently dressed in loungewear, happens to show up and reaches for the exact same thing... Oh, come on. As if that would ever happen! That's it. I'm out... That's honestly how it makes me feel!

And yet, I have to admit that the way the show gradually dissolves old emotional wounds, lingering resentment, and all that murky baggage from the past through these unexpected encounters is genuinely impressive. But as Koyun herself admits in the episode, she's incredibly sensitive to anything that might hurt her own feelings while remaining remarkably oblivious to other people's. She just keeps twisting everything around in her own head, making herself into an absolutely exhausting pain in the ass.

Another thing that struck me is how much the audience's emotional response can be manipulated simply by choosing how to present an event—what perspective to show it from, how to describe it, and what tone to use. I'm starting to wonder whether that's practically all this show does, in a way. And man, some of Koyun's facial expressions are just awful... Then there's that earlier scene at the family restaurant, with Minato conveniently saying what he did right next to them. These coincidences are really starting to bother me, and I'm getting tired of putting up with Koyun's endless emotional complications. So, despite recognizing just how exceptionally well-crafted this series is, I'm giving this episode an 8.

review.en:
Episode #4: The Troubles of a Young Man

"Okkoto-nushi, hordes of copy-pasted demons disguised as bears, and a brooding character whose reckless stunt left me shaking my head... What a waste of potential."

I don't think the story or its underlying ideas are bad at all. But I've come to realize, especially after watching this episode, that this is fundamentally a show about watching the beautiful Romelia face every hardship, crisis, and battle with her seemingly unshakable composure, then overcome it all through brilliant leadership and strategy. If you're the kind of viewer who enjoys that regardless of how conveniently or clumsily the obstacles are thrown into her path, then this might actually be a pretty good show for you.

The contrast between the two male leads is interesting enough, and so is Ray's struggle after discovering that he has magical abilities. He finally has a glimmer of hope and desperately wants to make himself useful, but his actions are so wildly impulsive and reckless that he completely disregards the trouble he's causing everyone else in the unit. I don't mind that development in itself, but I can't help thinking that, with better execution, material like this could easily have made for a 9-point episode.

Then there's the first half, where we get what looks like Okkoto-nushi from *Princess Mononoke*, only to watch these massive boars get slaughtered one after another. And in the second half, just when I thought we were dealing with bears, they turned out to be demons... appearing in yet another army of seemingly copy-pasted enemies. Oh, come on... I was seriously considering giving this a 7, but since so many other shows this season are downright awful, I'm settling on an 8. To be honest, even whether I'll keep watching this one is starting to feel pretty questionable.

"Am I already starting to get a little bored? I wouldn't quite call it repetitive yet, but I can definitely feel the early signs..."

I'm not entirely sure what to make of this episode. Nothing in particular really stuck with me, and the whole thing just felt a little... underwhelming. It's not that any specific segment was especially bad. Maybe the show is simply starting to feel a bit repetitive. Up until now, I've been enjoying the constant introduction of new characters and the surprisingly bold, outrageous ways it keeps pushing the boundaries. But inevitably, you get used to that sort of thing. And the whole getting-locked-in-the-gym-storage-room scenario—or rather, somehow managing to lock themselves in?—just made me think, "Oh, come on... I've had enough of this already."

Still, the overall quality remains high, and I'm enjoying it well enough. So I'm definitely not writing it off just yet. I'm still hoping it has plenty more surprises in store.

review.en:
Episode #52: (#4 This Season): The Last Volume

"The mystery surrounding the whereabouts of the other book and the side effects of the immortality elixir were fascinating, but the second half was... crap."

The first half was genuinely fascinating, with the mystery of where the other book ended up, the connection between the immortality elixir and its effects on memory and physical health, and the idea that there's no way that girl would have left without leaving something behind. I was really drawn into how all those elements were coming together. But then came the second half, with Jinshi acting like a spoiled, needy brat, the whole business with the facial sketch, and the courtesans' sympathy... What the hell was all that supposed to be? I honestly couldn't make much sense of it, and worse, it was just plain boring. The first half was good enough to barely earn this episode an 8, but if this happens again, it'll probably be a 7 next time.

review.en:
Episode #3: They're One and the Same

"Once again, everything is just a plot device. Funny how they keep running into exactly the right people at exactly the right time. Everything bends to whatever the story wants to show us. I've lost interest."

How am I supposed to care about any of this? Everything happens purely for the sake of whatever the writers want to show us, complete with these contrived, supposedly passionate emotional confrontations. Characters conveniently show up only when the plot needs them, and I can't bring myself to care about a single one of them.

This episode was no exception. Chinatsu just happens to walk past the dentist's office and starts thinking about Taiki—even though she was nowhere to be seen when Taiki actually went to the dentist. And then, wouldn't you know it, an old friend just happens to walk out at that exact moment, and they bump into each other! The moment I saw that, my immediate reaction was simply, "Yeah... this show is hopeless."

Aren't there way too many anime pulling this kind of thing lately? Or has it always been this way...? Somehow, though, this feels like a slightly different breed of contrivance. Whatever the case, this series seems to be nothing but one conveniently manufactured encounter or development after another.

第3話: 1つのことだよ

"相変わらず全部がプロットデバイス、よくばったり会うね、見せたいもののために全てが動く、興味なし"

review.en:
Episode #4

"Honestly, this is getting painfully stupid to watch. All the fiery passion in the world can't make up for this nonsense. Behold, Superhuman Takemitchy!"

I'm about ready to call it quits... So Takemitchy takes three bullets at point-blank range, then somehow manages to save a guy who's jumped off a rooftop with just one hand? Oh, come on... What is this, The Avengers?! And while he's still dangling there, screaming, "Help me!" we get yet another tearjerking miracle, where a handshake with Mikey suddenly lets him travel back in time? Give me a freaking break!

I don't know whether the writers deliberately set things up so that triggering this time leap was the only possible way for both of them to survive, or whether it was simply a convenient outcome brought about by Takemitchy's "resolve" and Mikey's desperate "cry." But honestly, I couldn't care less about any of that at this point. The execution and narrative structure are so poorly handled that whatever emotional impact they were going for is completely lost on me.

review.en:
Episode #3: Nightmare

"The animation is... low-quality and wildly inconsistent. How many studios are working on this thing? The story goes nowhere, it's not entertaining, and honestly, watching it is the real nightmare."

The animation... actually, pretty much everything about this production... Is it even okay? The quality varies so drastically from scene to scene that I have to wonder whether they've outsourced different parts to different studios. Not that even the better-looking parts are particularly good, mind you. I guess the male lead's flashback scenes were relatively decent. But more than anything, the story just refuses to move forward. Some woman shows up out of nowhere after apparently being transported here, and now she's traveling around with this guy. That's it. That's literally all that's happened. And we're already three episodes in...? Are you freaking kidding me?

Then there's the animation of MH's movements, especially when it's running. That scene where it apparently charges straight into an enemy and sends them flying? Holy crap, that looked awful. And somehow it can carry a man that huge? Come on, none of this makes any sense. Oh, and apparently the flying squirrel is *that* important, huh...? Seriously, I have no idea what the hell is going on here.

I gave this show a little credit last time, but... yeah, I don't think this is going to work out. I'll give it just one more episode to see if things improve.
review.jp:

"作画が・・・クオリティ低いしバラバラ、何社でやってる?進行しないし面白くもない、これが悪夢だよ"

entries.synopsis:
Noriko Tachiki has dreamt of a beautiful fantasy land for some time, though her friends think it is only her imagination. One day, on her way home, Noriko stumbles upon a bomb disguised as a paper bag that explodes right in front of her. However, instead of dying, she is transported to a mysterious forest full of strange plants and creatures.

As she begins navigating through the woods, Noriko is suddenly attacked by a giant, worm-like monster. Fortunately, she is saved by Izark Kia Tarj, a swordsman who does not speak her language. Lacking the strength to survive on her own, Noriko decides to follow her stoic savior, taking the opportunity to learn the foreign land's language and be more useful to Izark.

Unbeknownst to her, Noriko is a crucial piece of an ancient prophecy. She is "The Awakening"—a being destined to unleash the greatest evil known as the "Sky Demon." With influential people plotting to capture Noriko for her supposed powers, both she and Izark must fend for themselves and overcome a future laced with chaos.

[Written by MAL Rewrite]

時を同じくして、世界中では「破壊をもたらす“天上鬼”を目覚めさせる者が現れる」「どの国よりも早く手に入れろ」と囁かれていた。目覚めとは、そして天上鬼とは何なのか——その答えを知るかのように、イザークは典子を見て呟く。
「この娘を殺さなければならない」言葉も文化も異なる二人の間には、それでも少しずつ小さな絆が芽生えていく。
そんな二人は、やがて壮大な運命の渦へと飲み込まれていく——。
